articles.title: The End of the Internet
articles.author: Ben Thompson
articles.summary: The old Internet, where anyone could host a server is over, but it's just the final blow in an ending that has been coming for years. The future, though, is brighter than it appears.
articles.content_html:
Listen to this post:

Log in to listen

It was the summer of 2003, just weeks before I was set to move to Taiwan, that I decided to create a blog to document my journey. I had, at that point, had a GeoCities site, a Blogspot site, a site I built in Microsoft FrontPage and hosted…somewhere, so this was my fourth swing at the blog thing (it was the seventh that ended up being Stratechery). I was intrigued by a just-released piece of software that promised a five-minute install; it was called WordPress.

It did, I must confess, take me much longer than 5 minutes to install WordPress: it turned out I needed to learn how to create a MySQL database and configure PHP; once you had all of those component pieces in place, then yes, it only took 5 minutes to install!

I was thinking back to those days last week when news broke that every version of PHP had a critical bug that allowed for remote code execution on the host machine; Stratechery today still runs on WordPress, but that WordPress is managed by Pressable, an Automattic company. That meant that my site was patched before the vulnerability was disclosed, and it would be crazy for me — or anyone else — to do it any other way. It’s kind of insane to think that twenty-some years ago I was doing everything by hand without having any idea what I was doing, and that it was totally fine. That’s the Internet, though: an insane invention from a time that is, sadly, gone forever.

The End of Blogs

2003 was, roughly speaking, right around the beginning of the blogosphere; yes, blogs existed — Dave Winer, often considered the father of blogs, started Scripting News in 1997, after early experiments with a personal site called DaveNet; Justin Hall started Links.net in 1994; Jorn Barger coined the term “weblog” for Robot Wisdom, also in 1997, and the influential kottke.org started in 1998 — but it was the early 2000s when blogs suddenly seemed everywhere, particularly in the political space:

  • Talking Points Memo, Andrew Sullivan and Boing Boing launched in 2000
  • Instapundit, Little Green Footballs, and Dooce launched in 2001
  • Matt Yglesias, Daily Kos, Eschaton, The Volokh Conspiracy, Power Line, Gizmodo, Gawker, paidContent, and Daring Fireball launched in 2002
  • Ezra Klein, Marginal Revolution, ReadWriteWeb, and AVC launched in 2003

That political blogs featured so prominently speaks, I think, to both the power and peril of the Internet’s first transformation. Up to that point the Internet was mostly technologists, comfortable discussing the intricacies of text editors and programming languages with other nerds on BBSs, early forums, and mailing lists; it was the politically minded, however, that realized that the freedom to start your own publication that could reach everyone was a radical development. The goal was not to make money; it was to make a difference.

Originally these new publications were novel; what soon became clear, however, is that they were the tip of a wave of content that would dramatically expand the web. Newspapers had influence by being geographic monopolies; early bloggers gained influence by being the first to a new medium. Ultimately, however, the real winner of the web was Google: as the amount of content became abundant, Google offered not distribution — which was free — but rather discovery; indeed, it’s because distribution was free that discovery became the most important part of the value chain.

Many of those early bloggers made a decent amount of money from Google through its AdSense advertising program; by the end of the decade, however, the ads became more intrusive even as the payouts shrank, both because the inventory was limitless, and also because the most attractive ad slots were on Google Search. And so we saw one of the first examples of how the Internet fails: because everything is open, everyone has an opportunity, which means infinite competition, which is terrible for business.

For many years I rued the fact I wasn’t one of those early bloggers; a decade later, however, I realized that I was actually just in time for a much more sustainable business model: subscriptions. I wrote in 2015’s Blogging’s Bright Future:

It turns out, though, that there are more business models than simply advertising, as Sullivan himself sought to show. Sullivan was, for the last two years, supported by reader subscriptions to the tune of nearly one million dollars a year, and while many were skeptical of Sullivan’s efforts when he started, his ability to raise money shouldn’t have been a surprise: his is a singular voice — to put it in economic terms, Sullivan’s writing had a low elasticity of substitution — so people were happy to pay for something they couldn’t get anywhere else. Right there was the exact loyalty that Klein fears has been lost…

I am, of course, acutely aware that there is a tradeoff when it comes to the subscription business model: by making something scarce, and worth paying for, you are by definition limiting your number of readers. Stratechery, though, serves a niche, and niches are best served by making more from customers who really care than from milking pennies from everyone.

In short, the answer to drowning in abundance is to purposely limit your audience — to go small. That is an economic model that works, and notably, there are a lot of bloggers on that list who are using that model today. Blogging is alive and well, it’s just constrained, and thus worth paying for.

The End of Social Media

Google wasn’t the only Aggregator: a decade later there was a new means of discovery, which was social media. Now instead of searching for a site you could have a link shared directly to you, not just by email but on a site that served up interesting updates about whomever you chose to follow. And, for a period of time, followers could become friends. Stratechery’s fortunate timing was not just in terms of subscriptions becoming technically viable, but also the fact that Twitter was a community, not unlike the early Internet: genuinely interesting conversations happened in public, and you could reply-guy your way to broader distribution.

Social media was also free, however, and even easier to get started than a blog ever was; that meant that the amount of content was greater by many orders of magnitude. This meant that algorithms started to matter — Facebook had one relatively early, but it took Twitter much longer — and also anyone with any sort of prominence had to start taking a much more defensive approach. Community, sadly, doesn’t scale; any platform that is available to everyone starts out special and spirals from there. Ultimately, public social media sites became personal entertainment sites, tuned for engagement, culminating in TikTok, a social media site with basically zero social component.

However, that doesn’t mean social networking went away: in fact, I think that social networking is stronger than ever; the difference is that it isn’t public, but is rather in group chats. Group chats are familiar, they are high trust, they are, in many respects, the best of the Internet: even as technology atomizes us the group chat is the only place you can connect with people you care about, anytime and anywhere.

In other words, the redemption of social media was — just like blogging — to become smaller. The scaling that mattered for most people was not an ever larger audience, but a proliferation of infinite finite groups. Social media 1.0, even at its best, followed the 90-9-1 rule: one percent spoke, nine percent commented, and 90 percent lurked; the magic of group chats is not in giving everyone a voice, but a place where you feel safe to talk.

The End of the Internet

The PHP vulnerabilities were just two of a host of security issues last week alone; there were also:

  • Compromised intermediate CA private keys (although this was an example of sheer incompetence, not AI hacking)
  • Major new vulnerabilities in Node.js, GitLab, Java, and Cisco products
  • Breaches in LiteLLM’s supply chain and Railway developer platform

This is, believe it or not, only a partial list, and I expect things to only get worse. All of software is built on an inherently creaky human-authored foundation; the human factor meant the primary gate in all of software development was “Did it work?”, not “Is it secure from every possible privilege escalation or race condition?” or the myriad of ways that software can act in ways not intended.

The saving factor previously is that attackers were limited by human time and ingenuity as well; AI, however, has limitless time and the ability to substitute iteration for cleverness — and it’s getting pretty clever as well! It’s not a surprise that this wave of vulnerabilities is coming to light, and it’s going to get worse before it gets better — which I do, for the record, expect to happen; after all, the good guys have AI as well, and in the long run software will be better when it is (re)written by AI, and defended by agents continuously.

At the same time, what this entails is that the public Internet, to an even greater extent than now, will be a battle zone at best (i.e. social media), and a wasteland at worst (everything else). Some of this is economic, as AI consumes everything — both content and attention — without giving any of the traffic back that Google did, but it is also technical: it was already a dodgy proposition to stand up your own site or app, which was the very promise of the Internet, given the hacking risks; in the age of AI it’s madness.

It is sad. When I was a kid we called up BBS’s that were hosted in people’s homes; when I was in high school we downloaded music from public FTP addresses; when I was in college we set up our own websites. Anyone could set up a server, and that server was just as much a part of the Internet as any other server; that’s simply not viable any longer, even if you weren’t worried about making money. The Internet as we knew it is dead.

There are, however, green shoots of possibility, and once again the answer is to go smaller. When anyone can make an app, the answer is not to try and make a quick buck in the App Store; in fact, the surge in slop will make the market worse for everyone. Rather, it’s to make something for yourself and a small group of trusted friends and colleagues.

This is exactly what has happened at Stratechery: we have made a bunch of different apps, for everything from podcast production to task trackers to calendar management, none of which will ever be made available publicly. That doesn’t even include the apps made for oneself: I’ve created a bunch of different apps to manage my house and sports viewing: it turns out I had a lot of software-shaped holes in my life that suddenly I can fill without asking permission.

Software has always been different from physical goods in that its zero marginal cost nature meant it could scale to far more people; at the same time, the sheer amount of up-front effort involved in creating it meant that the intended audience needed to be large enough to justify the investment. AI completely changes that: suddenly it’s possible to create software for one person, or one team; smaller target audiences aren’t just a necessity for security, they’re an entirely new and potentially much larger market for software creation at scale, by literally everyone. Or, to use the example above, the group chat era of software is here and it’s going to be so much better than what came before.

Markets, Past and Future

Venkatesh Rao wrote an absolute must-read essay over the weekend called Cognitive Mercantilism. In brief, Rao makes the case that mercantilism rested on an assumption that economics was about scarcity and control; what brought about capitalism was demand. When people were freed from the burden of subsistence farming they discovered wants and desires at a scale that pulled entire markets into existence. Rao suggests the same might happen when people are freed from “subsistence cognition”. Rao concludes:

What gets missed is the possibility that we are witnessing the beginning of a transition as profound as the one from an overwhelmingly agricultural society to an industrial and commercial one. From a world where 80% of human brains are engaged in subsistence cognition to one in which 95% are engaged in satisfying previously unfulfillable cognitive demands.

The most important consequence of the agricultural revolution was not that farming became more efficient. It was that most people were liberated from the necessity of farming, allowing entirely new kinds of economic and cultural life to emerge. Likewise, the most important consequence of the AI revolution may not be that intelligence production becomes more efficient. It may be that most minds, human and eventually artificial, are liberated from the necessity of producing intelligence merely to survive, and become free to discover what they actually want to do with it.

The cognitive mercantilist sees a world threatened by an oversupply of intelligence and an impending surplus of useless minds. The AI Malthusian sees a world in which intelligence outruns the capacity of humanity to absorb it, leaving a growing population of economically redundant minds primed for revolutionary explosions. The cognitive capitalist sees the possibility of an almost limitless expansion of demand, and a world full of minds whose potential has barely begun to be explored.

I do understand why people have difficulty imagining this future. Capitalism, particularly over the last half century, has increasingly given way to scale, as ever larger corporations mediate ever more economic transactions, and as the Internet has played an important role in making the market a global one. The England in which capitalism emerged, however, and especially the America in which it was perfected, was much different. Alexis de Tocqueville, in Democracy in America, famously wrote:

The political associations which exist in the United States are only a single feature in the midst of the immense assemblage of associations in that country. Americans of all ages, all conditions, and all dispositions, constantly form associations. They have not only commercial and manufacturing companies, in which all take part, but associations of a thousand other kinds — religious, moral, serious, futile, extensive, or restricted, enormous or diminutive. The Americans make associations to give entertainments, to found establishments for education, to build inns, to construct churches, to diffuse books, to send missionaries to the antipodes; and in this manner they found hospitals, prisons, and schools. If it be proposed to advance some truth, or to foster some feeling by the encouragement of a great example, they form a society. Wherever, at the head of some new undertaking, you see the government in France, or a man of rank in England, in the United States you will be sure to find an association.

I met with several kinds of associations in America, of which I confess I had no previous notion; and I have often admired the extreme skill with which the inhabitants of the United States succeed in proposing a common object to the exertions of a great many men, and in getting them voluntarily to pursue it. I have since travelled over England, whence the Americans have taken some of their laws and many of their customs; and it seemed to me that the principle of association was by no means so constantly or so adroitly used in that country. The English often perform great things singly; whereas the Americans form associations for the smallest undertakings. It is evident that the former people consider association as a powerful means of action, but the latter seem to regard it as the only means they have of acting.

My life is defined by the Internet: I witnessed and participated in its evolution, and maybe in some small way contributed to it; I certainly owe my livelihood and success to it. I bemoan its passing.

And yet, in some ways, I am optimistic about what comes next. When it comes to economics, or social interaction, or now software, the only viable approach is to become smaller; smallness at scale, though, means there is not one global market, but infinite local ones. “Local” might mean geographic, or it might mean a private network; what many markets definitely means is many opportunities, because economies of scale matter less than the ability to meet new needs that only arise at the level of the association.

This is where I come back to de Tocqueville: the Internet is an American invention, and has long been defined by American mores; the individuals who thrive on the Internet, no matter their nationality, come across as very American in their iconoclasm and cringe. Beyond the individual, however, there is the association, and amongst the association there is not a market, but infinite markets. Markets are just another word for needs and desires and the mechanisms of meeting and fulfilling them; the end of the Internet may mean the possibilities for creation are only just beginning.

Presented by

When I write about tech companies, I am often writing about businesses that depend on Stripe, because Stripe provides the foundation for Internet-native companies — including Stratechery.

Consider Substack: building Stratechery was complicated and involved gluing together disparate pieces; Substack made it easy by delivering an integrated offering. One piece that was the same, however, was Stripe: Substack creators are also Stripe customers, as are creators on many other platforms.

Zoom out and the pattern repeats. Fintechs can build entire business models around card programs without ever having to build the issuing and processing infrastructure underneath it.

AI companies can charge for what customers actually use, which is particularly important when usage also drives costs, without having to build the systems to track and bill for it themselves.

No business succeeds because of Stripe. Stripe doesn’t answer the hard questions about what to build or whether anyone will actually use it. But it does make more things practical to try.

articles.title: 2026.43: A New Era
articles.author: Ben Thompson
articles.summary: The best Stratechery content from the week of October 19, 2026, including the best iPad but worst phone, SS Sarandos in a storm, and You Can See Everything.
articles.content_html:
Welcome back to This Week in Stratechery!

This week marks a new era for Stratechery, which is now presented by Stripe. I’m excited about what this partnership can unlock, starting with in-person on-video episodes of Sharp Tech. Check out the YouTube video above (or watch it on Stratechery); and, for subscribers, look forward to a bonus episode showing up in your subscriber feed every Sunday morning (add your feed on sharptech.fm).

Here were a few of our favorite topics this week:

  1. The Best iPad; The Worst Phone. John Gruber wrote a great review of the iPhone Duo, which we broke down on Dithering. In short, it’s an iPad that fits in your pocket, and it’s awesome at that; just don’t expect a good phone. Plus, on Monday we discussed Apple’s surprising partnership with Meta for edge AI, a topic I also covered in Tuesday’s Update. — Ben Thompson
  1. The SS Sarandos in a Storm. The past week has seen a flood of bad news for Netflix: layoffs, executive departures, another disappointing round of earnings, and another hit to a share price that has taken a 40% hit over the past 12 months. Wednesday’s Update provides a comprehensive state of the union, and we doubled back on the topic for a fun conversation on this week’s Sharp Tech, where we divided the company’s problems into areas that can be fixed (the content) and what may be much trickier (growing the business in a world where Meta and YouTube are primary engagement competition).— Andrew Sharp

  2. You Can See Everything, But Can’t Trust Anyone. Allow me to be the 1,000th person on the internet to recommend Nathan Fielder’s new Elizabeth Holmes documentary, You Can See Everything. After declaring on Sharp Tech last week that I wasn’t interested in seeing it, I did in fact check it out, and wound up loving it. I wrote about my experience on Sharp Text, with 5 spoiler-free notes for anyone still on the fence, and 5 more reactions for anyone who’s seen it. Compulsively watchable (and worth seeing in a theater), I think it may have also been the most effective document of our modern media environment I’ve ever seen. — AS

Presented by

It’s kind of weird to be the Internet’s number one fan of ads. What makes it even weirder is that I have been the Internet’s number one fan of ads without actually having ads on Stratechery.

That second part is changing: I’m super excited to announce that Stripe is going to be the presenting sponsor of Stratechery. And, at the end of the day, for me it couldn’t be any other company.

One of my hangups in terms of advertising is that I take my ethics super seriously, and ultimately, if a company is helping pay the bills, it’s hard to be truly objective about them. What I realized, however, is that it’s hard for me to be objective about Stripe anyway. 

I wanted to be a professional blogger long before I started Stratechery; however, I thought I had missed my chance, particularly as it became clear that advertising was not a long term business model for a one-person site. However, when Stripe launched with support for recurring billing, I realized there was a better model: subscriptions. 13 years later, and I’m still a happy customer. Or, to put it another way, I’m already conflicted because I love Stripe. 

I’m not the only one: more than 5 million businesses use Stripe, accounting for 1.7% of global GDP. Moreover, a lot of those businesses are Internet native and accretive to the world’s economy, which is to say that Stripe is literally making the world a better place. That’s an easy company to get behind, especially since they have been behind Stratechery from the very beginning. — Ben Thompson

Stratechery Articles and Updates

  • Do You Trust Apple? — Apple has a lot of trust in terms of delivering integrated products and preserving privacy; the real trust question is if you think Siri AI will justify investing more in their ecosystem.
  • Muse Spark Open, Meta + Apple, Thin and Thick — Meta has a new open source model, and to everyone’s surprise, they are are partnering with Apple to make sure you can run it locally.
  • Netflix Earnings, Business or Franchise, Disney’s Deal — Netflix has a solid business, which is exactly the problem: the company increasingly seems like a business and not a franchise, at least in terms of growth.
  • An Interview with Craig Moffett About SpaceX and Bubbles — An interview with Craig Moffett about SpaceX, from launch to broadband to mobile, plus how he is applying the lessons of the dot-com bubble to today.

Sharp Text by Andrew Sharp

  • You Can See Everything (And It’s a Great Time) — Nathan Fielder’s movie lives up to the hype and captures the modern world better than any art in recent memory.

Dithering with Ben Thompson and Daring Fireball’s John Gruber

  • Apple + Meta AI
  • The Duo Review

Asianometry with Jon Yu

  • The Birth & Rise of India’s IT Outsourcing Industry

Sharp China with Andrew Sharp and Sinocism’s Bill Bishop

  • New Export Controls in Multiple Sectors; Q3 GDP and the Fifth Plenum; Europe Presses Forward; OpenAI and Nvidia Chips

Greatest of All Talk

  • Aday Mara and the OKC Woodchipper, An Emergency Celtics Panic Watch, Silver Appreciation(???) and Laker Dreams

articles.title: Presented by Stripe
articles.author: Ben Thompson
articles.summary: Stratechery is now presented by Stripe. What that means for me, for you, and for the future of Stratechery content.
articles.content_html:
Listen to this post:

Log in to listen

Stratechery is, starting from today, presented by Stripe.

The Unified Content Business Model

Readers have, over the years, pointed out the paradox of my belief in and advocacy for advertising-based business models being delivered in a format bereft of advertising. In truth, however, there was no paradox, just pragmatism: when I launched the Stratechery business model I intended on having sponsors, and did for a month or two, before I realized that ad sales for a one-person business with a small audience was a waste of time; I was much better served devoting my attention to content and trusting that readers would be willing to pay.

And, thankfully, readers were willing to pay, and ultimately, there ended up being far more such readers than I ever dreamed of. In fact, there were so many readers willing to pay that I have, over the subsequent 12 years, been able to build an audience that is uniquely attractive to potential advertisers, along with a team that can help me pursue the multi-faceted business model I always planned on. Stratechery is a business, and subscriptions + advertising is The Unified Content Business Model I have long advocated.

Embracing Conflict

That noted, this is a big change, both for you and for me; I’ll start with the latter. I take my ethics policy very seriously, including the fact I am not paid for posts, I do not hold individual stocks, and I pay for all of my own expenses. This has, in all honesty, probably cost me a fair bit of money, but the payoff has been trust from you, and for me the sense of personal integrity this provided.

To that end, with this announcement, I am editing my ethics policy to include this paragraph:

Stratechery is, as of October 2026, presented by Stripe, and there I make no claims of objectivity. To the extent I analyze not just Stripe but the entire fintech space, I strive to give my honest opinion; my contract with Stripe contains total editorial independence. However, the reality of a conflict is inescapable, and I will disclose my relationship to Stripe in every post where this conflict may be relevant.

My ethics policy is going to include a link to this announcement, because there is one more admission to make: if I am honest with myself I have never been truly objective about Stripe specifically, for three reasons.

  • First, Stripe is a foundational business for my business. The then-startup launched the Subscription API (what later became Stripe Billing) in late 2011; Stratechery was predicated on that feature existing (and, I would add, the fact that a novice developer like myself could incorporate the Subscription API spoke to Stripe’s ease-of-use!).
  • Second, Stripe is the foundation of Passport, the access management software that undergirds Stratechery, SemiAnalysis’ institutional offerings, and The Ankler; we have and continue to work with Stripe closely for both Stratechery and Passport.
  • Third, I have had the good fortune of becoming friends with Patrick and John Collison, who were some of the earliest Stratechery readers and subscribers.

I did always try and set these considerations aside when writing about Stripe; in truth I actually just wrote about Stripe and the fintech space less, as I was cognizant about these informal conflicts.

By the same token, this is exactly why I couldn’t be more thrilled to have Stripe as an exclusive sponsor: if I am informally conflicted, why not make it formal? I actually think this gives me more freedom to write about fintech, not less, because the conflict will be on my sleeve; more than that, however, every ad I run or read is going to be heartfelt: I believe in Stripe, love their service, and while I am being paid for those ads, I will have the satisfaction of truly believing in them as well.

FAQ

That leaves the impact on you, the reader, and I’ve made an FAQ:

Where are ads going to run?

There are three primary places you will see Stripe ads:

  • There is a “Presented by Stripe” placement on Stratechery, the cover art of the Stratechery, Stratechery Interview, and Sharp Tech podcasts, and in the emails I send. I honestly think it looks pretty great, but I’m biased!
  • There will be occasional ad placements between sections of the Update, in the Interviews, and between Articles; this will apply to the web, email, and the Stratechery podcast (which is, and will continue to be, simply the audio version of what you can get on the web or via email).
  • There will be a segment of Sharp Tech where Andrew and I discuss the Stripe ad topic of the week, along with an acknowledgment at the beginning of an episode, and an ad at the end.

More on Sharp Tech below.

What about sponsored content?

There is no requirement that I run sponsored content; however, I’m actually very excited about the potential of occasionally leveraging Stripe content. Stripe has a unique position in terms of working with companies across the entire economy, and that is particularly true when it comes to AI. You see some of the insights that come from this position on both the Stripe blog and the Stripe Economics blog, and I look forward to incorporating those kinds of insights when it makes sense (and I should also call out Stripe’s Works in Progress site). Just to be clear, however, that will be my call.

So Stripe can’t tell you what to write?

Absolutely not. More than that, Stripe cannot tell me what not to write either. I could call for Patrick Collison’s firing and I’m still going to get paid.

I am not, for the record, going to do that; as I noted I will disclose this relationship whenever it seems relevant. However, my first loyalty is to my readers; that meant absolute editorial independence was a prerequisite for this deal.

Can I skip the ads if I’m a subscriber?

No. Like I said above, Stratechery is a business, and it’s the quality of my audience that makes this deal possible. Moreover, Stratechery has never promised to be ad-free: what I am selling is access to my paid content, and it’s on me to make that content worthwhile. In fact, I would spin this the other way: my motivation to deliver great content is higher than ever, knowing that it has to be worth not just your money but also the attention that I have chosen to share with a sponsor.

That noted, while I don’t make categorical statements about my business, I do not anticipate raising subscription prices again, and certainly not over the course of this deal.

Do I get anything out of this deal?

This is the part I’m most excited about: I am going to invest the revenue from this deal into making more and better products. I have a bunch of ideas that are now unlocked, and one of them is launching this week: in-person Sharp Tech.

The New Sharp Tech

I am extremely excited to announce that, starting this week, Sharp Tech will become a video podcast, recorded live and in-person. Over the past couple of months I have been building a small video studio in my home, and Andrew will be flying to Wisconsin every week (when possible) to make what I strongly believe will be a better product. There is no matching the energy and chemistry that comes from recording in person, so we’re going to do exactly that the majority of the time.

We will be posting video episodes on YouTube (for clarity, not live as we record, at least to start), as well as through existing feeds; these episodes will be free. In addition, we will be adding a second weekly mailbag-centric audio-only episode — recorded the same day, in-person — for subscribers only.

This is the first of what I hope will be many product launches for subscribers; my goal is that this sponsorship is seen as a real unlock and accelerant for what it means to be not just a subscriber but a member of the best audience in the world. That’s what I believe I have, it’s what Stripe believes that I have, and I’m grateful to every one of you for making that a reality and this business possible.

articles.title: Do You Trust Apple?
articles.author: Ben Thompson
articles.summary: Apple has a lot of trust in terms of delivering integrated products and preserving privacy; the real trust question is if you think Siri AI will justify investing more in their ecosystem.
articles.content_html:
Listen to this post:

Log in to listen

On July 21, 1999, Steve Jobs did something remarkable at Macworld New York: first he went to Apple.com, then to “CNN Interactive”, then to Disney.com. That wasn’t the remarkable part: what blew the crowd away was when he picked up the just-introduced iBook and walked around while waiting for Disney.com to load. The crowd went wild at the lack of wires:

I’m not going to quote this entire product introduction, but I’ve clipped the whole thing for your enjoyment; here are a few pertinent parts of Jobs’ introduction of what he called “AirPort”, and what the rest of the industry called “WiFi”:

There is one more thing.

The main point of this keynote was the aforementioned introduction of the original iBook:

This meant that “one more thing” was in fact not just an extra unexpected product, but an explicit addition to the primary product’s feature set.

No wire. What is going on here? We are really excited to announce, in addition to iBook, AirPort wireless networking…It’s a wireless LAN. It runs at 11 megabits per second, and it’s based on industry standards. This is 802.11 wireless networking, and everybody is jumping on board with this thing over the next six to nine months. So all sorts of devices are going to be able to interact with AirPorts. We’re just going to be there first and best, and the specification also incorporates quite a bit of privacy protection, so everything you send out is encrypted. A lot of privacy. We’ve worked with Lucent on this for the last 18 months, hand-in-hand to marry their wireless technology with our ease-of-use technology and to bring the cost of this down for people, because this stuff has been pretty pricey to date.

Apple’s selling proposition has, in many respects, never changed: modern technology that is easy to use and private too.

So AirPort, what is it? This is the first thing: this is the AirPort base station, and it looks like this, right like that, and so the AirPort base station is really cool…

And, of course, industrial design:

So what about the computer side of things? Well, iBook is the first computer ever designed right from the start to be optimized for wireless communications, and so right in every iBook are two built-in antennas…Then, we have an AirPort card, a small little card, and the iBook is designed to accept it. So let’s take a look at that. As you know, Apple pioneered this way of adding memory without taking your whole portable apart through simply lifting the keyboard. Well, we have enhanced that now to take an AirPort card, and as you see, there’s a space right there in every iBook ready for an AirPort card, and you can drop one in, just like that, and connect the cable that comes from the antenna. Right? You saw that? I’ll go back. Just connect that cable and push it in, and now your iBook is AirPort functioning. You are on the wireless network. All the software detects the AirPort card and automatically sets it up for wireless networking without going through hours of configuring your computer. It all happens automatically. This has been a major effort on the part of Apple’s hardware and software engineers and also Lucent.

This paragraph is a bit extraneous, other than the fact it is personally meaningful: my first Apple computer was an iMac G4, the following all-white generation, with the same AirPort card installation. I remember being amazed at just how easy it was to add wireless. And now, here I am, 22 years later, still using an Apple laptop to write this Article.

Apple HomeView

Two weeks ago I wondered how long I was for the Apple ecosystem; one product I was definitely not interested in was the then-forthcoming Apple smarthome product:

What struck me about Gurman’s article is just how unenthused I am by an Apple smarthome product. Some of this is fatigue from a decade of Siri disappointment and skepticism about the company’s ability to deliver on a voice-centric product. More than that, however, I bristle at the idea of introducing Apple’s constraints to more parts of my life.

Those constraints aren’t just about things like full disk access. To the extent that Apple delivers on integration with things like thermostats and door locks is the extent to which they work with 3rd-party device makers; the problem is that third party device makers mostly suck, particularly from a software perspective. Even if Siri were perfect, Apple will have the challenge of delivering an experience that isn’t defined by the lowest common denominator.

What I’m much more interested in is controlling the software layer myself. The fact of the matter is that with AI you can decompile almost all existing software — there is a revolution happening in gaming over the past few weeks, as game after game is decompiled to source and ported to any platform you wish — and you can write your own. That means my software that interacts with my agent in the way I want it to for everything; that’s way more exciting than praying Apple delivers the right API and that 3rd-party developers don’t suck.

That product is called Apple HomeView, and some prominent Apple observers don’t get the point. John Gruber wrote on Daring Fireball:

My skepticism boils down to the question of why anyone would want to add one (or more!) additional ever-present screens to our homes and lives. Phones can stay in our pockets until we need them. Watches remain on our wrists. HomePods can be tucked away unobtrusively in corners, and remain fully useful. HomeView needs to be in a prominent location for its display to serve any practical purpose. Apple’s initial pitch for it doesn’t earn that prominence for me.

I understand Gruber’s skepticism, particularly given the product’s truly atrocious introductory video. Beyond the overall stress-inducing nature of the suburban family scene depicted, most of the use cases, as Gruber notes, are nonsensical: to take a particularly egregious example, why would the teenage daughter look at a message from her clandestine boyfriend on the HomeView instead of her iPhone (which has to be present on the network and unlocked in the past several hours for that functionality to even work)? Apple was, in this particular case, trying to show off HomeView’s multi-user capability, which is based on facial recognition, but my biggest takeaway is that maybe highly produced marketing videos sold as product keynotes aren’t the worst idea in the world.

In fact, I think that HomeView is pretty compelling. Smarthome functionality is genuinely useful:

  • Years ago I set up a small monitor on the side of our condo’s living room for the kids to play video games; I happened to have a Raspberry Pi on hand, which I used to set up a service called DAKboard. DAKboard showed the time, the weather, the family calendar, and a rotating collection of photos. It has, in the intervening years, been one of our most-used and most-beloved pieces of technology, looked at multiple times a day every day.
  • Thermostats are finicky and hard to use; it’s much better to be able to program them from your phone, or from a touch device. The problem for me in my current home is that my thermostats seem to mysteriously lose their connection to my home automation system every few weeks.
  • Doorbells are critical in a world of e-commerce, especially when it comes to the dreaded “signature required”; incorporating them with your devices, along with a screen to see who is at the door, is a no-brainer. Unfortunately for me my doorbells also seem to get randomly disconnected, and I never notice until I miss a delivery.
  • Cameras are a useful security measure, but only if you can actually view them. The issue is — you guessed it — that they often become inaccessible or are non-intuitive to use, particularly the moment you need them.
  • Sometimes I want to access information without using my hands, like when I am cooking. You can prop up an iPhone or iPad in the kitchen, but what do you do when it goes to sleep in the middle of a recipe?

I have, of course, just laid out five compelling use cases for the HomeView, but it wasn’t hard! These are all real, genuinely useful capabilities for a new home device. And notice what the limiting factor is for the middle three: actually getting different devices to work together reliably.

Apple’s Trust Dividend

That’s why the other exciting part about Apple’s HomeView announcement actually hearkened back to the original AirPort: Apple Home Collection. From Apple’s press release:

Apple today announced Apple Home Collection, a new lineup of smart home accessories — including indoor and outdoor cameras, thermostats, temperature sensors, and a video doorbell and door lock — designed in collaboration with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. These new accessories are simple to set up starting with one tap with iPhone, and everything is managed through the Apple Home app — no separate app or account required. Each accessory is encrypted end-to-end in Apple Home, so only users and the people they choose can access their home data.

Building on the thousands of Works with Apple Home and Matter accessories available today, Apple Home Collection offers customers a new array of recommended products to better understand what’s happening inside and outside their home, manage access, and keep the temperature just right throughout the day. Availability for all products begins in December, with select accessories available starting early 2027.

“Apple Home Collection makes it easy to choose smart home accessories with confidence,” said Matthew Costello, Apple’s vice president of Hardware Engineering. “Working closely with industry leaders LG Electronics and Schneider Electric, we designed every accessory to work seamlessly with Apple Home, so managing your home is simple, reliable, and private.”

Apple doesn’t have to do everything itself in the home, just as they didn’t have to invent wireless networking in 1999; what they need to do is “marry [partner’s] technology with [their] ease-of-use technology”, and I’m optimistic they’ve done exactly that with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. The key detail is “no separate app or account required”; that points to deep integration with Apple products, from setup to day-to-day usage.

Again, I’m not sure I’m the target customer for this (although the automatically unlocking door locks look awesome); my solution to incompatible or flakey integrations is to use AI to build my own customized software. I’m under no illusions, however, that I am a normal consumer who wants the benefits of technology without the headaches; I trust Apple, more than anyone else, to at least aspire to delivering on that vision, and these 2nd-party partnerships are a great start.

The second part where you may trust Apple more than any other company is with privacy. Jobs was talking about privacy as a selling point 27 years ago, and Apple has only doubled down since then. In the case of HomeView specifically there is that facial recognition feature, tied to your own hardware; more broadly, if there is any company you might entrust with tracking your more private spaces it is Apple, both because of promises they make with their technology and also their consistent stance on not using customer data. Indeed, Apple’s privacy umbrella is strong enough that LG’s very sketchy privacy track record is likely to be a non-issue amongst potential customers.

Apple’s Trust Deficit

From Bloomberg, in 2016:

Apple Inc. has disbanded its division that develops wireless routers, another move to try to sharpen the company’s focus on consumer products that generate the bulk of its revenue, according to people familiar with the matter. Apple began shutting down the wireless router team over the past year, dispersing engineers to other product development groups, including the one handling the Apple TV, said the people, who asked not to be named because the decision hasn’t been publicly announced. Apple hasn’t refreshed its routers since 2013 following years of frequent updates to match new standards from the wireless industry. The decision to disband the team indicates the company isn’t currently pushing forward with new versions of its routers. An Apple spokeswoman declined to comment on the company’s plans.

The official end of the line came in 2018, five years after the last product was released, leaving customers in limbo waiting for updates that never came. That right there is one reason to not trust Apple in the home: the company already decided once that products that didn’t move the needle relative to the iPhone weren’t worth their time, even if delivering an integrated home experience was still something Apple was uniquely positioned to provide.

Yes, by the 2010s most people had WiFi access points from their ISPs, or mesh WiFi products from the likes of Eero, but Apple still could have done something useful. For example, one of the biggest challenges in designing a wireless network is that the iPhone aggressively holds onto access points; if Apple had continued to design its own access points it could, even today, provide a superior experience. Alas, the business was deemed to be not big enough to bother.

One reason Apple might be more interested this time, however, is the possibility of subscription revenue. Specifically, the cameras in Apple Home Collection will require a paid iCloud+ plan for recorded event history — higher levels for more cameras — which fits in with the company’s focus on services. Apple Music is also natively supported on the HomeView, whereas you’ll need a recently unlocked iPhone to use Spotify. Of course to some this might be another betrayal of trust: Apple used to sell you products, now they want to sell you on-ramps to recurring revenue.

Both of these issues of trust, however, pale in comparison to the single biggest question facing HomeView: do you trust Siri to actually work?

In Siri We Trust (or Not)

From Mark Gurman at Bloomberg:

Apple Inc.’s new HomeView has been a long time coming — far longer than the company intended. I first reported on the device in January 2023, when Apple was aiming to bring it to market as early as the end of 2024. What should have been a relatively straightforward launch instead turned into a nearly two-year saga of delays. The culprit was Apple’s AI crisis, which left the company without the one piece of technology the HomeView absolutely needed: a working version of its revamped Siri assistant…

From the beginning, the HomeView was built around a Siri that could retrieve personal content, distinguish between members of a household and show each person private information. It was also designed to be controlled primarily by voice, rather than through its touch screen. Without a serviceable version of the new assistant, Apple couldn’t deliver the experience it had envisioned. That left the hardware ready to go, but the software nowhere near finished.

So Apple postponed the HomeView repeatedly — first until spring 2025, then summer, then fall, and then again throughout 2026 before finally unveiling it this past week. And the hardware betrays its age. With thick bezels, an A18 processor and 8 gigabytes of memory, this is clearly a product conceived years ago. Finished units have been sitting boxed up in warehouses for the better part of a year, waiting for the software to catch up.

There is a world where Apple never gives up on AirPort, and instead uses it as a foundation to deliver the integrated smarthome in the late 2010s; in that world Siri’s performance is important but also less pressing given that some number of homes would already be locked in.

The second world, which Gurman describes, is one where Apple delivers on the new Siri in 2024 like it planned, and the HomeView is its showpiece experience. This is still a compelling product in that scenario, where integrating information from your iPhone is close to the cutting edge of what AI is capable of.

The world we are in in 2026, however, is a much different one. In this world Siri AI has shipped, and while it is more capable than what came before, it is much slower, and makes more mistakes with basic tasks that the deterministic old Siri handled reliably. Moreover, the competitive landscape is dramatically different: agents like Muse, Instinct, Dots, or Grok Bots not only integrate information but actually act on it; new Siri already feels long in the tooth.

This is where a foray into the home is particularly challenging. One doesn’t replace one’s thermostat or cameras or doorbells every year; these are one-time purchases meant to last for a long time. Ditto cutting a hole in your wall to mount a HomeView, which certainly makes more sense for many of the product’s core use cases. Making such a commitment, however, means committing to Siri AI as the primary interface, and trusting that Apple will make it good.

This is a costly choice, and not just monetarily. The real concern is opportunity cost: committing to a world controlled by Siri AI means forgoing a world controlled by any other AI. That’s too expensive for me; how many consumers, even those who trust Apple to make things work together, and who value the company’s commitment to privacy, will make a similar evaluation?

Cook’s Costs

The answer right now, in 2026, is probably not too many, which is to say Apple might have got this product out just in time. I think there is something here, even if Apple’s marketing team doesn’t seem to be able to explain it very well.

At the same time, I think HomeView highlights some of the mistakes and shortcomings of former CEO Tim Cook’s tenure; earlier this year when Cook retired I wrote about his impeccable timing, both in terms of when he took over Apple, and also when he stepped down:

To that end, it’s right that Cook is stepping down now. Jobs might have been responsible for taking Apple from 0 to 1, but it was Cook that took Apple from 1 to $436 billion in revenue and $118 billion in profit last year. It’s a testament to his capabilities and execution that Apple didn’t suffer any sort of post-founder hangover; only time will tell if, along the way, Cook created the conditions for a crash out, by virtue of he himself forgetting The Cook Doctrine and what makes Apple Apple.

The Cook Doctrine states that Apple needs “to own and control the primary technologies behind the products we make”, but Apple doesn’t own and control the models underlying Siri; meanwhile, one of the things that makes Apple Apple is focusing on making great products that customers love. How did Apple’s obsession with services revenue fit in that rubric, particularly when said obsession rose in conjunction with stripping out every part of the business that didn’t move the needle in terms of revenue, even if it made for a better user experience? Privacy, meanwhile, is great as a strategy credit; what happens when it gets in the way of making products that work?

It is true that Apple’s AI approach has the benefit of not moving the needle in terms of costs, at least relative to its big tech peers. It’s possible that just as Apple is partnering with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric on home devices, the company will deliver compelling experiences through its partnership with Google (and surprising thawing with Meta via its Meta Superintelligence Lab). After all, Apple hasn’t always done everything — Lucent Technologies once featured in a Steve Jobs keynote!

The difference is that that was an Apple that was eager to race ahead, not simply catch up; Jobs was planting seeds for the future, seeds that Cook harvested. Cook did make investments that matter, particularly in Apple Silicon (even if that effort started under Jobs), and in wearables; the job for Ternus will be ensuring that Apple’s “ease-of-use” technology is not just easy but actually useful.

Welcome back to This Week in Stratechery!

As a reminder, each week, every Friday, we’re sending out this overview of content in the Stratechery bundle; highlighted links are free for everyone. Additionally, you have complete control over what we send to you. If you don’t want to receive This Week in Stratechery emails (there is no podcast), please uncheck the box in your delivery settings.

On that note, here were a few of our favorites this week.

  1. What is Apple Doing? On last week’s Dithering, John and I bemoaned Apple’s exit from home appliances in the 2010s; now the company is back and John doesn’t see the point. I think a big problem was Apple’s marketing video; after I explained what Apple was trying to accomplish on Sharp Tech Andrew was almost persuaded to go all in on HomeView. — Ben Thompson
  1. SpaceX Continues Eating and Expands Its Appetite. Elon Musk and SpaceX have continued their spectrum buying spree, and in Tuesday’s update Ben broke down the implications of both the latest deal, as well as recent deals that mobile carriers (and airlines) have done to avoid reliance on SpaceX. This market’s dynamics are fascinating to me, and for SpaceX, what once looked like a play to become the de-facto provider of emergency satellite coverage among mobile providers now looks like a company that’s coming for primary cellular coverage. Come to read about the methods that could make that path viable, and stay to appreciate challenges that make it a quintessential Musk strategy. — Andrew Sharp

  2. Titles, Takes, and the Washington Wizards. The NBA season begins next Tuesday, and if you want to have a good time preparing this weekend, we’ve got you covered. First, Greatest of All Talk makes the case for eight different potential title winners (although I must warn you that our Knicks repeat case was extremely unconvincing) and runs down our favorite highlights from the preseason. Then, for Friday’s Sharp Text, I played the most dangerous game of all and expressed confidence the Washington Wizards (for the first time in a full decade) while also offering 18 more takes and predictions for the rest of the league. — AS

articles.title: A Conversation With Ari Emanuel About Entertainment and AI
articles.author: Ben Thompson
articles.summary: A conversation with Hollywood super-agent Ari Emanuel about his memoir, the impact of AI on Hollywood, and the power of a phone call.
articles.content_html:
Listen to this post:

Good morning,

This week’s Stratechery Interview ended up not being an Interview, but rather a conversation with Hollywood super-agent Ari Emanuel. Emanuel is the Executive Chairman of WME Group, Executive Chair and CEO of TKO Group Holdings (the owner of UFC and WWE), and Founder of MARI, a live events and experiences company.

The occasion for this conversation née interview was the recent publication of Emanuel’s memoir, Roll the Calls, a reference to Emanuel’s relentless daily phone call routine; I got on Emanuel’s roll for the first time a couple of years ago, and quickly learned that when Emanuel wants something he gets it.

That’s a theme of his book, and of this interview: Emanuel decided he wanted to have a conversation and ask me some questions too, so that’s exactly what we did. We cover everything from the state of social networks, AI’s impact on Hollywood and the tech industry, and what skills might not just persist but become more valuable. We also discuss why Emanuel is making such a big bet on live, whether or not Hollywood is logical, and whether talking on the phone is the antidote to polarization.

As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player.

On to the conversation:

A Conversation With Ari Emanuel About Entertainment and AI

This interview is lightly edited for clarity and content.

Topics:

The State of Social | Roll the Calls | AI and Creativity | Buying UFC | Post-AI Tech | AI and Generational Change | MARI | Hollywood Logic

The State of Social

Ari Emanuel: Can I ask you one question? Because I saw your interview. Who was it — you did it with a guy in New York.

Patrick O’Shaughnessy?

AE: Patrick, yeah, who I love.

Yeah, I read your interview with him, it was great.

AE: I loved your point of view, and explain a little bit more to me because I love your thinking — that on a SaaS model, the only one, based on my understanding, based on your model right now, that’s got it right, OpenAI should have gone to advertising as opposed to charging, Muse has it right.

Yeah, for sure.

AE: They don’t need to charge you because they have the other revenue stream.

Right. And well, not just that, but the LLM, like, it’s actually really interesting. So when they launched Muse, they made this promise, “We won’t use your data that you use with Muse for advertising”, and no one cares. No one knows they made that promise, and no one cares, because no one cares about that stuff. And so they, in some respects, handicapped themselves by making this promise.

AE: Just like Apple, we’re not going to look at your data, major mistake when Tim [Cook] said that.

Right. But in the long run, I think it’s going to pay off, because you’re going to have this complete change in how advertising works. Right now you sort of have data on the user and you have data, broadly speaking, of what a particular product matches with and you’re matching, it’s called the two-towers approach. So you’re matching these two things together, and that’s how advertising basically works at scale, and it’s all these vector databases, all these sorts of things.

AE: Television never did it properly.

That’s right. So the way advertising is going to work in the future, and it’s already happening, is it’s going to predict what you want.

AE: Well, the funny thing, what I thought when you said that—

(laughing) I can never remember if I’ve said it before.

AE: One is, Mark is going to be able to make a ton personally and charge, he’s going to be able to use the AI to do it, and it’s going to be just more and more and more.

It’s more than that. So what you’re going to do is you’re going to get a personalized ad predictor that basically is inside your VM. They’re going to be credibly able to say it’s totally private, because it is totally private.

AE: Because it’s just directed at you.

That’s right, it’s just predicting what you want to see. Just like it’s going to be a predictor of content you want to see.

AE: Oh, I didn’t think about it that way, yeah.

The reason why there’s such massive upside is this whole agent thing — this is the real Google threat. So everyone thought when ChatGPT came out, that was a threat to Google, but the human was still in the loop. As long as the human is still in the loop, Google is okay. But all of Google Search, Amazon search—

AE: Once the human is out of the way…

Then all these search-skim ad models, which is what all these models are, they’re all bullshit models, because it’s just attacks on search.

AE: Well, are you saying the same thing about Amazon?

Yeah, 100%.

AE: I think Amazon, because of Muse — I mean, Walmart made the deal with them.

Which is a huge deal.

AE: Amazon’s going to have to figure out — I mean, a lot of stuff is going to go through.

Well, and the problem is that the problem with having a physical moat is that means you have a lot of capital tied up in that, which means you do have a forcing function that means you have to adjust.

AE: It’s what happens when you’re just saying that when you have a digital, not a personal, on the Amazon side, your $60 billion is in jeopardy on your advertising business. I mean, it’s a problem.

It’s a big problem, a huge problem for them. So the upside is the new products still need advertising, and things like live events, all the sorts of personalized stuff that the Internet makes possible. Like, one of the most important functions is going to be the generation of human desire, that is the post-AI economy.

AE: MARI! That’s exactly how I think about it. It’s like, you know, not only what Elon [Musk] said to me — it can’t be disintermediated.

Don’t waste it. We’re going to get to it. I get to talk now, you don’t get to talk, because I have to record this for the interview.

AE: I can’t believe we’re not recording now!

I am recording, but I didn’t say we hadn’t started yet, so maybe we can include this. We should make this more of a conversation.

AE: We can just go. This is the interview.

Okay, this is the interview, we started.

AE: Exactly how my life goes.

Okay, I’ll throw away my script here.

AE: The reason I love talking to you is this, I can’t articulate it as well as you can.

You have this massive need for the generation of human desire, and you’re going to have people like you who are creating the vessels in which to sort of collect that human desire. But that means that advertising has just been between 1% and 2% of GDP, so let’s say that holds.

AE: Oh, it’s going up more.

It has gone up with digital, yeah, it’s up to between 2% and 3% now, but historically, it’s been between 1% and 2%.

AE: I think it’s going to above that.

I think it will too. So this is the conservative estimate. Amazon advertising is impaired, and Google advertising is impaired, because there’s no more human in the loop, that advertising is going to flow to surfaces that are not impacted by AI.

AE: Facebook.

Facebook.

AE: I couldn’t think, after that conversation you had with Patrick, if there’s another group out there, and maybe it’s X? Because I think Elon’s going to do that, right? But I didn’t think of another one, another kind of digital player that could do that, except maybe Microsoft inside LinkedIn.

Which, by the way, is doing very well.

AE: Very well. Because actually that is a digital personal because people are involved.

I think social networks are only going to get more valuable over time, not less.

AE: I agree.

If anything, we’re almost at the nadir of social network value.

AE: So name the social networks in the United States. Facebook. Instagram. X. And I said LinkedIn. Did I miss one?

No, I don’t think so. So that’s the brilliant thing about Muse, it’s not only this phenomenal opportunity, it’s also a direct heat missile at Meta’s competitors, to the extent it lands, and that money’s going to flow back into Meta.

AE: And I think it actually — depending on what [Amazon CEO] Andy [Jassy] does, who’s very smart, he’s got to make a deal. Over time, he’s got to figure out that $60 billion, which is one of the biggest problems.

Here’s one thing that’s interesting, and I’m curious what you’re thinking about it. So in the long run, of course, AI is very highly deflationary but I think there’s an aspect that it is short-to-medium-term inflationary, in that ads are a subsidy to the people who are not impacted by the ads. Stuff is cheaper, Amazon is a good example — the prices Amazon charges are definitionally less than they would be absent advertising. And we know this because their advertising revenue is more than their e-commerce revenue — or their profit, I should say.

AE: And the advertising does subsidize all that.

That’s right. So if the advertising goes away and they have to charge more, that is actually inflationary to a certain extent, because prices have to go up. And I think you’re going to see this — like, for example, what’s a very easy Muse use case? Find these subscriptions that are lingering, what subscriptions do I have that I should cancel? There’s a lot of advertising businesses that are supported by people forgetting to cancel their subscription.

AE: This is the same argument I’ve been making with people. The cable business — ESPN was elevated not because so many people were watching it, there was that select group of people that had to have it, and then they could get up to $10 for it.

And everyone paid it.

AE: And once that broke with Netflix, etc., it just went away. The cable operators and cable were broken, it just fell to the ground.

Yep, and you have to pay directly for sports, so sports fans were the biggest welfare recipients in history throughout the entire cable era.

AE: And now they’re going to pay for it, but advertisers are going to pay premiums for it, because it’s a very high-end group of people that they want, on whatever platform they have.

All the video advertising, streaming advertising — particularly to your point, if they actually finally do it right. And which, by the way, Amazon is probably the furthest ahead there, generally speaking.

AE: I think [Skydance CEO] David Ellison will catch up. He hired the right CTO out of Facebook, and he’s going to build a pretty good model. The one place — would you define YouTube as a social network? It’s in between, right?

What is a social network? So is Instagram even a social network anymore? It is, to an extent. But the big shift, and the reason why TikTok sort of blindsided Meta, is TikTok is classified as a social network, but it’s not a social network at all, it’s a user-generated content network.

AE: Well, so is Reels.

That’s right, and Reels is a direct response to realizing, “Holy cow, we missed it”.

AE: And the issue is that, unlike Threads, Reels works.

There’s this famous Paul Krugman article that’s saying the Internet is not going to have any more economic impact than a fax machine.

AE: He said that?

Yeah. Maybe it was a long time ago, I wrote about 2014, he must have said it in the late ’90s, early 2000s or something. And the reason is because most people don’t have anything interesting to say and the funny thing is he was actually half right and you saw this with what happened to Facebook. As long as your content was limited to people you knew, it was fun.

AE: Everybody cared!

They came to not care, because what happened was TikTok realized, if you’re limiting what people see to only the people you know, they’re not seeing the best stuff. What the TikTok algorithm does is it basically finds the best content across the entire service, and feeds it to you, such that it’s the best content in the world — even though the percentage of good content to bad content is hilariously small. The vast majority of content sucks, but the absolute value of good content is very large, because the total amount of content is so great, even if you get a very small number on a massive denominator. And so they’re like, “We’ll just show you the best content”.

AE: And that’s what their algorithm did, they could figure that out.

That’s right, and that was Meta’s blind spot, because they killed Snapchat by leveraging their network. You already had friends — you could see a story on Instagram, and it was instantly useful to you, because you were already following people on Instagram.

AE: But why — I want to ask you a question, and this brings up Snapchat. Why hasn’t he [Snap CEO Evan Spiegel], as opposed to doing glasses, figured out he is one of the last social networks? And it’s still good. He’s got a billion users.

(laughing) There’s a lot of good questions that can be asked about Evan Spiegel‘s corporate governance, most of which are not very flattering.

AE: I mean, he is one of the last social networks, we’re talking about social networks — he’s one of the last ones, and he actually still has a great user base.

He does, and it’s still young.

AE: Very young, and they use it to talk to people.

The engagement is off the charts. If you use it, you use it all the time.

AE: And if he did it right with AI, as opposed to the glasses

I mean, this is the eternal Snapchat question. That’s why they are still such a lure to investors, despite the fact they pay out gazillions in stock-based compensation, they never seem to really make money, blindsided by Apple a few years ago, and all these sorts of things, is because it’s so clearly a tremendously valuable asset.

AE: And completely utilized by a generation.

Yeah, absolutely. So, yes, Snapchat is always a question.

AE: So now let’s get to the advertising piece on live. Because my opinion is the following, let’s just say you were right, 1% or 2%.

By the way, this is a perfect framing for this interview, where you just sort of took it over. I think we’re actually conveying, at a meta level, the experience — the Ari Emanuel experience. So anyway, continue.

AE: (laughing) Well, it’s kind of the experience, I’ve been reading your newsletter, and I just call you out of the blue, and we start talking.

Roll the Calls

Well, your book is Roll the Calls.

AE: You got one of them! I rolled you!

You did. It kind of made me scared for this interview when I was actually reading the book, I’m like, “do you actually stop for an hour and not talk on the phone?”.

AE: Yeah, because it’s an interesting conversation, I’m going to learn something.

I did remember the first time you called me.

AE: You were in Asia, weren’t you?

No, I was in Seattle the first time you called me, but I was still living in Asia. And the second time I was in Asia, I missed your call in the middle of the night. But what was striking is your assistant emailed me, I found the email asking for my phone number which says, “Ari wants to call you”. I replied, and I think my phone rang within 30 seconds, which was stunning to me.

AE: (laughing) Were you sleeping, and you had woken up and got there?

No, it was Microsoft Build, it was in May, so I was there. I think I was going to interview [Microsoft CEO] Satya [Nadella]. I was in the lounge at the Hyatt downtown getting breakfast.

AE: Oh, wow. I don’t remember what the conversation was about.

It was some Article I wrote, I don’t remember what it was.

AE: I didn’t understand it completely, and I wanted some answers.

Do you still talk on the phone as much as you did back in the ’80s?

AE: Oh my god, yeah. I don’t like this whole thing. Ron Meyer once said to me, we were talking about this — and he still reads papers, and I read papers online — and he said, “You know, if texting existed before telephones did, and then all of a sudden telephones came out, people would be calling people as opposed to texting”, because the reverse happened, texting’s cool, and people just do that. So yeah, I’d rather have a conversation.

The bandwidth is just higher.

AE: Especially for me — one, being dyslexic. Two, the misinterpretation, potentially. Larry David can write funny texting, I can’t do that.

Well, I think what’s interesting is, I mean, a lot of the book is — and you talk about this — just sort of your not giving up, I think, is a generous way to put it. Asking a million times, you mentioned the dyslexic angle, not being embarrassed, people can keep saying no — it doesn’t bother you. But I think there’s an aspect of that relentlessness combined with, in a phone call, because it’s so much higher bandwidth, you get the shape of the problem or the shape of the person much more clearly and so that pressure you’re putting on is also much more finely targeted.

AE: When I get on a phone call, like I just hung up with Marc Andreessen about something, and I didn’t understand something he was asking me, I was asking him a question. I just want the answer to that one thing. I’m not sitting here — it could be 14 calls, because I might have multiple calls, but in each situation I don’t have a long conversation. I just don’t understand something, I want an answer, I’m going to the people that I think have an answer.

That answer, for whatever my life is going on, answers some question that I want answered, to kind of continue a conversation or understand something so I can think about what we’re doing, how we’re thinking about this. This is one of the reasons I wanted to do this — because one, I love your newsletter, I read it, as you know, consistently, but I was wondering, AI, live — your point of view on it.

I have a point of view — one, that people are going to have more free time, they’re going to come to it. But also, I think there’s going to be the ability to put it on social and I think advertising in arena is going to go pretty high, because you’re concentrated and I think that’s true for both TKO and I think that time that people have now is going to be so much more precious, they’re going to have more money — we can talk about that — and it’s just like where the world’s going.

So is it “Mari”? Is that how you say it?

AE: Do you know how that name came about?

I do not.

AE: I have a Monday morning weekly call with all the executives at TKO — WWE, UFC, everybody — and we were going over, I don’t know, an advertising issue or a site fee issue and the executive goes, “Mari!”, I go, because Mark Shapiro was talking — I go, “What did you just say?”.

Oh, it was Mark and Ari.

AE: I lost my shit on him, it was hysterical, then I had shirts made with “Mari” — Mark and my face combined, it was really funny, so that’s how it came.

You mentioned, as far as the thesis, people are going to have more free time, live events are going to become more valuable.

AE: And what were you just saying about your point of view about people’s time and events? You were just talking about.

I agree. And I think there’s a second layer, which is I can relate to — you just have a question, you want to get answered. You came up in like the age of the world talking on the phone so of course you’re going to call someone to get the answer.

AE: Or somebody that I think has thought about it maybe differently than me, that I could — would make me change an opinion or add to my opinion.

Right. Well, but in the ’80s, you’re an agent, you needed to know everything that was going on and that was the original purpose of rolling the calls. So I obviously am younger than you.

AE: It’s not obvious that you’re younger.

(laughing) I know, you do look great. These are your barbells and your famous walking treadmill. So Google came out when I was in college, it was unbelievable, it was so much better than everything else. But even before then, you go back to me being a kid, and like having the encyclopedia at home, or having the dictionary. Every time you encounter a new word, go look it up, every time you encounter a concept, look it up. This aspect of just always, if anything comes up that I don’t know, “Get the answer!”. AI obviously takes this to the extreme — do you ever ask AI for any of your questions?

AE: All the time. I was having this conversation — maybe this is way too political. I just didn’t understand why people, both on the far left and the far right, were using the phrase “genocide” as it relates to Israel and I said, “How the F did that work?”, there was that book about how words were created, I forgot the name of the book, long time ago I read it.

So I used Grok, and it said, “This guy, 1944, a lawyer, family went through the Holocaust, etc”, and I’m like, they’re trying to take a word that was created because of a genocide, by a Jew, and make it their own — the whole thing blew me away, we all constantly use it.
